messages.subject: Extract Sampler Parameters in RStan
parts:
I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again, not having sampler parameters
(accept stat, n divergent, etc) included in extract by default is dangerous.
The user should be forced to look at these Clockwork Orange-style.

But I also can’t figure out how to access them from a stanfit object at
all (there’s no official doc on how to do this and the archived users
list is no help). Seriously, why is this so hard?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extract Sampler Parameters in RStan
parts:
The magic key you're looking for is:

get_adaptation_info

It IS in the doc.

> On Mar 2, 2015, at 11:58 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again, not having sampler parameters
> (accept stat, n divergent, etc) included in extract by default is dangerous.
> The user should be forced to look at these Clockwork Orange-style.
I agree that these should be included in extract, just like lp__.

> But I also can’t figure out how to access them from a stanfit object at
> all (there’s no official doc on how to do this and the archived users
> list is no help). Seriously, why is this so hard?

In the doc for stanfit-class, you see:

get_sampler_params
signature(object = "stanfit"): obtain the parameters used for
the sampler such as stepsizeand treedepth. The results are returned
as a list, each element of which is an array for a chain. The array
has number of columns corresponding to the number of parameters used
in the sampler and its column names provide the parameter names. Optional
parameter inc_warmup indicates whether to include the warmup period.

Here's an example:

> fit <- stan(model_code = "parameters { real y; } model { y ~ normal(0,1); }")

> samp_params <- get_sampler_params(fit);

At this point, samp_params[[1]] is the first chain, samp_params[[2]] is
the second chain and so on. Each chain has everyting in order.

> head(sps[[1]])
accept_stat__ stepsize__ treedepth__ n_leapfrog__ n_divergent__
[1,] 4.781267e-01 2.0000000 1 1 0
[2,] 1.860020e-218 5.5698093 1 1 0
[3,] 9.682160e-01 0.7105644 3 5 0
[4,] 8.290335e-01 0.7877146 2 3 0
[5,] 9.444573e-01 0.7123420 2 3 0
[6,] 9.966285e-01 0.9768503 1 1 0

If you want to get rid of warmup, use

get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)

but you probably don't for these since you've said we should be
paying attention to n_divergent__ in warmup.

It's in the R doc, but not under what you may be looking for,

This kind of doc issue (not knowing how the stanfit object was constructed
so not knowing what's in it by design) is one reason I don't like having single
classes or functions overloaded for different types of return types.
There's no way to provide clean doc for the get, because the columns
will vary based on the type of sampler (e.g., NUTS has treedepth__ but
vanilla HMC doesn't). Similarly, stan() is used for the call for both vanilla
HMC and NUTS. Just like in the command line.

- Bob

On Monday, March 2, 2015 at 9:39:09 AM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
How did you get  the doc for the stanfit class?  I tried
all of the method()-like functions I could google but
the best I could get was

"> methods(class='stanfit')
[1] as.array.stanfit*      as.data.frame.stanfit* as.matrix.stanfit*     dim.stanfit*          
[5] dimnames.stanfit*      is.array.stanfit*      pairs.stanfit*         print.stanfit*        

   Non-visible functions are asterisked"

Those aren't the methods you are looking for. More specifically, those are the S3 methods. You want the S4 methods, but you can't get them by doing

showMethods("stanfit-class")

because S4 methods are defined for generic functions with S4 classes as signatures instead of being part of the classes definition (like every other object-oriented language and the S4.5 classes in R, a.k.a. reference classes, which are not currently used by RStan but I am in favor of converting to). The shortest path to what you want probably would have been to look at all the functions exported by the rstan package and then guess what they do.

> ls("package:rstan")
 [1] "constrain_pars"      "extract"             "get_adaptation_info"
 [4] "get_cppcode"         "get_cppo_mode"       "get_cxxflags"
 [7] "get_inits"           "get_logposterior"    "get_num_upars"
[10] "get_posterior_mean"  "get_sampler_params"  "get_seed"
[13] "get_seeds"           "get_stancode"        "get_stanmodel"
[16] "grad_log_prob"       "log_prob"            "lookup"
[19] "makeconf_path"       "monitor"             "optimizing"
[22] "plot"                "read_rdump"          "read_stan_csv"
[25] "rstan_options"       "sampling"            "sflist2stanfit"
[28] "show"                "stan"                "stanc"
[31] "stan_model"          "stan_rdump"          "stan_version"
[34] "summary"             "testify"             "traceplot"
[37] "unconstrain_pars"

And then was does get_sampler_params return?  It’s
a list of what, exactly?  typeof() claims that it’s a double,
but it’s single-indexed and it’s not at all clear how to
extract a single sampler parameter.

It is a list whose length is equal to the number of chains. Each list element is an iterations x 4 matrix. It works almost like a std::vector except that you have to index it with double brackets. So,
my_list <- get_sampler_params(posterior)
my_list[[1]][2,3]
extracts the first list element and then the element in the second row and third column of that matrix. Typically, you would want to apply the same function to each chain, in which case it would be something like
sapply(my_list, FUN = colMeans)

Ben

Here's a function that will return the max treedepth for each chain. If you change "treedepth__" to any of the other sampler params and change "max" whatever function you want then you can pretty much get any sampler param info you want using this template. 

max_treedepth <- function(stanfit, inc_warmup = TRUE) {
  max_td <- sapply(get_sampler_params(stanfit, inc_warmup = inc_warmup),
                   function(x) max(x[,"treedepth__"]))
  names(max_td) <- paste0("chain", 1:length(max_td))
  max_td
}

If you don't feel like writing each of those functions, I've already done most of them for you and whole bunch of others. There's a handy little convenience function in the shinyStan package called stan_get that you can call from R.  See help("stan_get", "shinyStan").
